rv.q: He is also trapped, unfortunately, inside an ambitious but awkward production whose elements battle one another more often than not.
The problem is, the production simply cannot find the right balance between these two stories, one a towering work of fiction, the other a sadly earth-bound biographical narrative.
Mary Shelley's Frankenstein's reach may exceed its grasp, but enough of its disparate parts connect to make it a reasonably stimulating and occasionally insightful experience.
There are fine ideas within Mary Shelley'S FRANKENSTEIN, but stronger dramaturgy and deeper execution are required to bring them to life.
The overall show is less than the sum of its parts.
Spectacular by Off-Broadway standards, Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein never gels into an arresting theater piece.
Wolf – and Fairchild – deserve monstrous credit for providing another look at and dimension to this oft-told tale of science and creativity gone awry.

The story and this production is as lost as that Monster flailing around in the woods.

You long for his dance moments and the thrilling Swann along with the musicians but have to deal with not only the pain of listening to dialogue delivered by three performers devoid of any conviction along with desultory writing and equally meandering direction.

cn.t: Fairchild's mesmerizing physicality and stunning classical music can't overcome this ambitious but disjointed multimedia production, where awkward performances and muddled storytelling leave critics admiring the concept more than the execution.
